intro: Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra play the opening of the Waltz of the Flowers from the Nutcracker Suite, where a free harp cadenza leads into a horn melody. This is the first disc side of their 1934 recording.

sections.label: Intro · Wind chords and harp cadenza
sections.mNote: The harp plays a cadenza in broken chords before the waltz.

sections.label: A · Horn waltz theme in D major
sections.mNote: The horns play the melody over a three-beat accompaniment.

sections.label: B · Waltz theme continued, longer phrases
sections.mNote: Long melodies continue above the bass and offbeat chords.

sections.label: C · Later phrases of the first side
sections.mNote: The waltz continues after the opening exchange between horns and clarinet.

cues.title: Harp cadenza before the waltz
cues.text: The harp’s long solo comes after the opening wind chords. Its arpeggios rise and fall freely before they come to rest on held chords. The bass then begins the regular waltz accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Jurgenson score, plate 17668, pp. 3–5: introduction, harp cadenza and a tempo waltz accompaniment. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Principal melody, horns and clarinet
cues.text: The horns play the principal melody in D major, marked dolce cantabile. A solo clarinet plays figures around their phrases. Below them, plucked bass notes and two string chords mark the three beats of each bar.
cues.evidence: Jurgenson score, plate 17668, pp. 5–6: horns, solo clarinet and string accompaniment. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recording, Camden, New Jersey, 1934
cues.text: In 1934 Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra recorded the waltz in Camden, New Jersey, at the former Trinity Church studio. The original record divided the dance between two sides, and this is the first.
cues.evidence: Recording year, Camden Church Studio No. 2 (Trinity Church Studio), performers and part 1 designation: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:PDP-CH_-_Philadelphia_Orchestra_-_Leopold_Stokowski_-_Nutcracker_Suite,_Opus_71A_-_Tchaikovsky_-_Waltz_of_the_Flowers,_Part_1_-_Hmv-db2542-2a87004.flac

cues.title: Place in the ballet and suite
cues.text: On stage, the flowers dance late in Act II of The Nutcracker, before the pas de deux. Tchaikovsky placed their waltz last in the concert suite.
cues.evidence: Ballet and suite movement orders: https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=The_Nutcracker and https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/The_Nutcracker_(suite).

composer.epithet: Composer who could write a brilliant ballroom scene and, within it, a single melody showing that someone present was unhappy.
facts: School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck: an allowance, 1877–90, and a friendship conducted by letter
Three ballets; Eugene Onegin, The Queen of Spades and other operas
composer.background:
At Kamenka on 6 July 1878, Tchaikovsky was explaining to Nadezhda von Meck how he composed. Ideas came to him in the middle of conversations, and he kept them in his head until he could sketch them on the first sheet of paper to hand. He held that waiting for the right mood was no way to work. “Inspiration is a guest who does not like to visit the idle,” he told her. He then stopped for dinner. At two o’clock he resumed, and went on to sketching, orchestration, fair copies and how far a symphony must keep to its traditional form.

He was born in Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. He grew deeply attached to his French governess, Fanny Dürbach, and began piano lessons at the end of 1845. The profession chosen for him was the law. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg. Four years later his mother died of cholera. He graduated in 1859 and took a post at the Ministry of Justice, while giving more and more of his time to opera and concerts.
